'''Rodney H. Banks''' (born January 14, 1953) is an American industrial [[chemist]] and a research fellow at [[Nalco Holding Company]] in [[Naperville]], [[Illinois]], now a wholly owned subsidiary of Ecolab Inc.  His inventions have greatly improved the control of industrial [[water treatment]].{{citation needed|date=February 2013}} In 2011, Banks received the [[Perkin Medal]] for his work from the American section of the [[Society of Chemical Industry]], the highest award for applied chemistry in the United States.<ref name="Society of Chemical Industry">{{cite web|title=. Society of Chemical Industry page listing Perkin Winners|url=http://www.soci.org/Awards/America-Group-Awards/Recipients-Perkin.aspx|accessdate=7 February 2013}}</ref>

==Early life and education==
Banks was born in [[Long Beach, California|Long Beach]], [[California]], on January 14, 1953, and later moved with his family to Maryland. His father Mark worked as a chemist for the [[U.S. Defense Department]] in Washington, D.C., inspiring the younger Banks to pursue the same field. Banks attended [[Johns Hopkins University]], graduating with a [[bachelor's degree]] in chemistry in 1975. In 1980, he received his [[Ph.D.]] in [[Inorganic chemistry|inorganic]]/[[physical chemistry]] from the [[University of California, Berkeley]], where he worked for [[Nobel laureate]] and fellow Perkin medal winner [[Glenn Seaborg]] on the [[Chemical synthesis|synthesis]] and [[Characterization (materials science)|characterization]] of volatile [[actinide]] compounds.<ref name="Naperville Sun article">{{cite news|last=Sharos|first=David|title=Nalco chemist earns Society of Chemical Industry Award|url=http://www.suntimes.com/business/5812933-420/nalco-chemist-earns-society-of-chemical-industry-award.html|accessdate=7 February 2013|newspaper=Naperville Sun|date=June 6, 2011}}</ref>

== Professional life ==
Banks moved to the Chicago area in 1980, working briefly as a post-doctoral student at [[Argonne National Laboratory]] on [[X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy|x-ray photoemission spectroscopy]] properties of [[neptunium oxide]]s before joining Nalco Chemical Company as a research scientist.

In the mid-1980s, Banks and other Nalco researchers identified opportunities for improved monitoring and control of water used in many industrial systems, especially in [[cooling tower]]s, for both commercial and office buildings and in industrial plants such as [[paper mill]]s, [[oil refineries]], [[Automotive industry|automotive plant]]s and [[steel mill]]s. He and colleague John Hoots subsequently led the invention and commercialization of fluorescent tracing technology, trade-named TRASAR. Banks' work involved using chemical and mechanical sensors for improved monitoring and control. The 3D TRASAR version of this technology won a United States Presidential Green Chemistry Challenge Award for its cooling water application in 2008.<ref name="Green Chemistry Award">{{cite web|title=2008 Greener Reaction Conditions Award|url=http://www.epa.gov/greenchemistry/pubs/pgcc/winners/grca08.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080715041324/http://www.epa.gov/greenchemistry/pubs/pgcc/winners/grca08.html|url-status=dead|archive-date=July 15, 2008|work=US EPA Green Chemistry Award|publisher=United States Environmental Protection Association|accessdate=7 February 2013}}</ref>

Banks has created various electrochemical, optical, quartz crystal microbalance-based sensors to measure chemical treatment levels, corrosion, scale and microbial fouling. He holds more than 30 U.S. patents.<ref name="Patent Listing">{{cite web|title=Rodney H Banks - Inventor|url=http://patent.ipexl.com/inventor/Rodney_H_Banks_1.html|publisher=Intellectual Property EXchange Limited (IPEXL)|accessdate=7 February 2013}}</ref>
